summary: Mayurasharma founded the Kadamba kingdom c. 345 after breaking with the Pallavas of Kanchi, making Banavasi the capital of the first native kingdom of what is now Karnataka. It reached its height under Kakusthavarma, who tied his family by marriage to the Gangas, the Vakatakas and, by some accounts, the Guptas; around 455 it split into Banavasi and Triparvata branches, which were reunited c. 530. Soon after, c. 540, the rising Chalukyas of Badami overthrew their former overlords, and Kirtivarman I later annexed Banavasi itself.
details: According to the Talagunda pillar inscription, Mayurasharma, a native of Talagunda, went to Kanchi, the Pallava capital, to study the Vedas. Humiliated there by a Pallava horseman, he gave up scholarship for the sword, built up a following in the forests of Shriparvata, defeated Pallava guards and made the Banas of Kolar pay tribute. The Pallava king reportedly recognised him as ruler of the land between the western ocean and the Malaprabha river. From his capital at Banavasi he ruled c. 345–365, founding the earliest native kingdom of present-day Karnataka, and performed horse sacrifices.

Mayurasharma's son Kangavarma came to the throne around 365. The Vakatakas, the most powerful dynasty of the central Deccan, pressed on the young kingdom from the north. Historians disagree about the outcome: one view holds that he was defeated by the Vakataka king Prithvisena but kept his independence, another that his war with them had no lasting result. His son Bhagiratha, called lord of the Kadamba land in the Talagunda inscription, may have recovered earlier losses, although Vakataka records do not confirm this.

Bhagiratha's son Raghu died fighting the Pallavas, and his brother Kakusthavarma became king around 435. Historians regard his reign as the height of Kadamba power. He built a web of marriage alliances: one daughter married Madhava of the Western Ganga dynasty, another, Ajitabhattarika, married the Vakataka prince Narendrasena, and according to one historian a third married the Gupta emperor Skandagupta. These ties linked the Kadambas of Banavasi with leading houses of central and northern India. Tradition says the poet Kalidasa visited the Kadamba court, probably in Bhagiratha's time.

A stone found in 1936 at the village of Halmidi in Hassan district is usually dated to about 450, though some scholars place it as late as the 6th century. Written in verse in pre-Old Kannada, it is described as the oldest known Kannada inscription. It records a grant of villages by two local governors to a prince, Vija-Arasa, for his military service, and names a King Kakustha, often identified with the Kadamba Kakusthavarma, though some epigraphists disagree. It is an early example of Kannada being used in government, alongside the Sanskrit of royal charters.

Kakusthavarma's son Santivarma, said to have worn three crowns as a sign of his prosperity, presided over the great Talagunda pillar inscription; his court poet Kubja composed and engraved it, telling the story of Mayurasharma. Santivarma's display drew Pallava attention, and around 455 he divided the kingdom: his younger brother Krishnavarma I took a southern branch, called Triparvata, while the senior line kept Banavasi in the north. Krishnavarma's sons later claimed that he had performed a horse sacrifice. The two branches ruled side by side, and in the end as rivals, for about 75 years.

In the Banavasi line, Shivamandhatru ruled for more than a decade from about 460, and Mrigeshavarma followed around 475. He fought the Pallavas and the Western Gangas with considerable success; his Halasi plates call him a destroyer of the Ganga family. He was also a patron of Jain institutions, continuing the Kadambas' support for several faiths. Meanwhile in the southern Triparvata branch, King Vishnuvarma is reported to have accepted Pallava overlordship, a sign of how the division had left the southern Kadambas exposed to their powerful eastern neighbour.

Ravivarma, who ruled roughly 485–519 (some lists say 497–537), restored Kadamba strength. He campaigned against the Pallavas, the Western Gangas and the Vakatakas, and a record from Davanagere dated around 519 is taken by the epigraphist D. C. Sircar as evidence of broad overlordship. He also granted land to a Buddhist community. Ravivarma left his brothers Bhanuvarma and Shivaratha to govern Halasi and Uchangi. His son Harivarma came to the throne around 519, according to the Sangolli inscription, and is described as a peaceful ruler.

The rivalry between the two Kadamba branches ended in bloodshed. According to the Bannahalli plates, Krishnavarma II of the southern Triparvata line raided Banavasi and killed King Harivarma around 530. With the senior line gone, the two halves of the kingdom were reunited under Krishnavarma, who had become the most prominent ruler of his branch. The reunion came late, however. In the north, the Chalukyas of Vatapi (Badami), a family that had served the Kadambas, were gathering strength and would soon turn on their overlords.

Around 540 the Badami Chalukyas, who had been vassals of the Kadambas, conquered the kingdom, and the Kadambas in turn became vassals of the Chalukyas. Historians debate how the Chalukyas rose: K. A. Nilakanta Sastri thought their leader Pulakeshin I began as a Kadamba vassal and won independence by taking control of the Vatapi area, while others see him as a feudatory of a different house who took over former Kadamba territory. Later princes of the Triparvata line, such as Ajavarma and Bhogivarma, are still listed into the early 7th century.

Pulakeshin I, the first sovereign Chalukya king (c. 543–566), proclaimed his independence in the grand manner. An inscription at Badami dated 543 records that he performed the Ashvamedha horse sacrifice, a claim to supreme kingship, and he made Vatapi his fortified capital. His son Kirtivarman I (c. 566–592) finished the work: he annexed the old Kadamba capital, Banavasi (Vaijayanti), and the Aihole inscription of Pulakeshin II later called him 'the night of doom' for the Kadambas. Kadamba rule as an independent kingdom was over, though later Kadamba families ruled Goa and Hangal for centuries.
